items.stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. A team builds a new feature that answers requests for the path /convert. The team wants a serverless solution, so that no instances need to be managed for this feature. The requests and the responses are small JSON documents. The rest of the application must stay unchanged. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: no instances need to be managed

options.text: Create a Network Load Balancer with a target group of type lambda, register the AWS Lambda function, and send the requests for the path to it.
options.why: Network Load Balancers cannot hold this target group, because Application Load Balancers are [the only load balancers that support](../facts/elb.md#elb-lambda-target-alb-only) the lambda target type.
options.misconception: believes that every load balancer type can invoke a Lambda function

options.text: Launch an Amazon EC2 instance that receives the requests for the path from the load balancer and invokes the AWS Lambda function for each request.
options.why: It works, but the proxy is one more instance to patch, scale and pay for, which the serverless requirement wanted to avoid.

options.text: Create a target group of type lambda, register the AWS Lambda function in it, and add a listener rule that forwards the path to the target group.
options.why: [The target is a Lambda function](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-target-types-instance-ip-lambda) in a target group of type lambda, and a listener rule sends the path there with no instance to manage.

options.text: Create a Gateway Load Balancer in front of the AWS Lambda function, and route the requests for the path through a Gateway Load Balancer endpoint.
options.why: A Gateway Load Balancer is for [deploying inline virtual appliances](../facts/elb.md#elb-gwlb-faq-when-inline-appliances) such as firewalls, not for running application code behind a path.
options.misconception: uses the load balancer for inline appliances to call a function

items.explanation: Application Load Balancers are [the only load balancers that support](../facts/elb.md#elb-lambda-target-alb-only) the lambda target type. [The target is a Lambda function](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-target-types-instance-ip-lambda) when the target group has the type lambda, and a listener rule for /convert forwards the requests to it. The function runs with no instances, and the other listener rules stay unchanged.
items.takeaway: A path of an Application Load Balancer can run a Lambda function through a target group of type lambda.
items.twin: If the stem said "each request uploads a video of several hundred megabytes" instead: keep the path on instances or containers, because a Lambda target takes a request body of at most [1 MB](../facts/elb.md#elb-lambda-target-body-max-1-mb).
items.say: Point an ALB rule at a lambda target group; the function answers the path, and nobody manages instances for it.

solvers.stem_only: Put the code in an AWS Lambda function, create a target group of type lambda on the existing ALB, and add a path-based listener rule /convert that forwards to it; the other rules stay as they are.

items.stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an internet-facing Application Load Balancer that has its own security group. A security audit finds that the instances are in public subnets with public IP addresses. Their security group allows HTTP on port 80 from 0.0.0.0/0. The company must remove every network path from the internet to the instances. The instances must accept HTTP requests from the load balancer and from no other source. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements in the MOST secure way? (Select TWO.)
keywords: public subnets with public IP addresses
remove every network path from the internet to the instances
from the load balancer and from no other source

options.text: Create a network ACL for the instance subnets that allows inbound HTTP only from the current IP addresses of the load balancer, found with a DNS lookup.
options.why: Elastic Load Balancing updates its DNS entry so that [IP addresses can be remapped quickly](../facts/elb.md#elb-dns-ttl-60-seconds-remap), so today's address list stops matching.

options.text: Move the instances to private subnets, launch them without public IP addresses, and keep them registered in the target group of the load balancer.
options.why: Load balancers reach targets [using private IP addresses](../facts/elb.md#elb-targets-need-no-public-ip), so the instances need no public address, and the internet has no path to them.

options.text: Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with each EC2 instance, and add a rule that blocks every request that does not come from the load balancer.
options.why: A web ACL protects resources such as [Amazon CloudFront, Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancer](../facts/waf.md#waf-protected-resource-types), and an EC2 instance is not one of them.

options.text: Keep the instances in public subnets with public IP addresses, and allow HTTP in their security group only from the CIDR block of the VPC.
options.why: The public addresses stay, and every resource in the VPC can still reach the instances, so they accept requests from more than the load balancer; targets [do not need public IP addresses](../facts/elb.md#elb-targets-need-no-public-ip).

options.text: Change the security group of the instances so that it allows HTTP only from the security group of the load balancer, and remove the 0.0.0.0/0 rule.
options.why: With [the load balancer's security group as the source](../facts/elb.md#elb-target-sg-reference-lb-sg), the instances accept requests from the load balancer and from nothing else.

items.explanation: Two controls work together. Load balancers send requests to targets [using private IP addresses](../facts/elb.md#elb-targets-need-no-public-ip), so the instances can sit in private subnets. A rule with [the load balancer's security group as the source](../facts/elb.md#elb-target-sg-reference-lb-sg) admits the load balancer and nothing else, even when its node addresses change.
items.takeaway: Targets belong in private subnets, with a security group rule that names the load balancer's security group.
items.twin: If the stem said "the application serves employees on the corporate network through AWS Direct Connect" instead: an internal load balancer, because its nodes [have only private IP addresses](../facts/elb.md#elb-internal-nodes-private-ips-only).
items.say: Put the instances in private subnets, and let their security group trust the load balancer's security group, not an address range.

solvers.stem_only: Two steps: move the instances into private subnets with no public IP addresses (they stay registered in the ALB target group, so the internet path is gone), and change the instance security group to allow HTTP only from the ALB's security group (security group reference) instead of 0.0.0.0/0. Not a NACL with ALB IPs (they change), not a VPC CIDR rule (too broad), and WAF does not attach to EC2 instances.

items.stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. Sometimes the application process on an instance hangs. The EC2 status checks of that instance still pass, and the load balancer marks the target as unhealthy. The instance stays in service for days until an engineer terminates it by hand. The company wants to automate the replacement of these instances. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: EC2 status checks of that instance still pass
the load balancer marks the target as unhealthy

options.text: Lower the unhealthy threshold of the target group health check, so that the load balancer terminates and replaces the hung instances sooner.
options.why: On a failed check, [Elastic Load Balancing stops sending traffic to it](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-checks-reroute-and-replace); the load balancer itself terminates and launches nothing.

options.text: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that runs an AWS Lambda function every minute to terminate the instances that the load balancer reports as unhealthy.
options.why: It works, but the team writes and maintains code for a check that the Auto Scaling group performs after one setting change.

options.text: Increase the deregistration delay of the target group, so that in-flight requests finish before the load balancer removes the hung instances.
options.why: The delay waits so that in-flight requests can finish when a target leaves; it detects no hung process and launches no instance.
options.misconception: confuses the draining of in-flight requests with the replacement of an instance

options.text: Turn on Elastic Load Balancing health checks for the Auto Scaling group, so that instances that fail the load balancer health check are replaced.
options.why: With the ELB health check type on the group, [Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling replaces the unhealthy instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-checks-reroute-and-replace) without any code.

items.explanation: By default, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling [ignores the results of the Elastic Load Balancing](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-health-checks-ignored-by-default) health checks, so a hung instance with passing EC2 status checks stays in service. For the ELB health check type, [you must turn it on](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-elb-check-must-be-turned-on) for the group. After that, [Elastic Load Balancing stops sending traffic to it](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-checks-reroute-and-replace), and [Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling replaces the unhealthy instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-checks-reroute-and-replace).
items.takeaway: The load balancer routes around an unhealthy target; an Auto Scaling group with ELB health checks replaces it.
items.twin: If the stem said "the instances are not in an Auto Scaling group" instead: nothing replaces them, because on a failed check [it stops routing traffic to that target](../facts/elb.md#elb-unhealthy-target-stop-resume) and launches nothing.
items.say: Turn on ELB health checks for the Auto Scaling group; then Auto Scaling replaces what the load balancer marks unhealthy.

solvers.stem_only: Set the Auto Scaling group health check type to ELB so that the group replaces instances that fail the target group health check, not only the EC2 status checks.

items.stem: A company runs six small web applications in one AWS Region. Each application has its own domain name, its own Amazon EC2 instances and its own Application Load Balancer. Each load balancer has an HTTPS listener on port 443 with an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate for its domain. Traffic to every application is low, but the load balancers run all day. Users must keep reaching each application at its current URL. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: keep reaching each application at its current URL

options.text: Keep one Application Load Balancer for each application, and lower the idle timeout of each load balancer so that unused connections close sooner.
options.why: Each load balancer is billed for [each hour or partial hour](../facts/elb.md#elb-partial-hour-billed-as-full-hour) that it runs, so six hourly charges stay; the idle timeout changes none of them.

options.text: Replace the six load balancers with one Network Load Balancer that has six TLS listeners, one listener on a different port for each application.
options.why: A Network Load Balancer works at [Layer 4](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-layer-per-type) and does not read host names, so each application needs its own port, and the URLs change.
options.misconception: expects one port per application to keep the current URLs

options.text: Keep one Application Load Balancer for each application, and turn off cross-zone load balancing on each target group to avoid data transfer charges.
options.why: With an Application Load Balancer, [you are not charged](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-cross-zone-no-data-transfer-charge) for regional data transfer of cross-zone traffic, so this saves nothing.
options.misconception: believes that cross-zone traffic of an Application Load Balancer adds data transfer charges

options.text: Use one Application Load Balancer with one HTTPS listener that holds all six certificates, and add host-header rules that forward to six target groups.
options.why: Host conditions [route requests to multiple domains](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-host-conditions-many-domains-one-lb) on one load balancer, and the certificate list lets one listener [support multiple domains on the same port](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sni-certificate-list-multiple-domains).

items.explanation: Each load balancer is billed for [each hour or partial hour](../facts/elb.md#elb-partial-hour-billed-as-full-hour) that it runs, so six load balancers bring six hourly charges. One Application Load Balancer can [route requests to multiple domains](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-host-conditions-many-domains-one-lb) with host conditions. Its HTTPS listener can [provide a different certificate for each domain](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sni-certificate-list-multiple-domains) through a certificate list. Users keep their URLs, and five of the six hourly charges go away.
items.takeaway: Several HTTPS domains can share one Application Load Balancer through host rules and a certificate list.
items.twin: If the stem said "the applications accept raw TCP connections on their own ports" instead: one Network Load Balancer with a listener per port, because it works at [Layer 4](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-layer-per-type).
items.say: One ALB with host rules and a certificate list replaces six load balancers, so the company pays one hourly charge instead of six.

solvers.stem_only: Consolidate onto one ALB: one HTTPS listener on 443 with all six ACM certificates (SNI), host-header rules forwarding to six target groups, and point each domain's DNS at the shared ALB.

items.stem: A solutions architect reviews the design of a new internet-facing TCP application on Amazon EC2 instances. In the design, a Network Load Balancer has one subnet, in Availability Zone A, and all the instances run in Availability Zone A. The application must be highly available and must keep serving clients if one Availability Zone fails. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: one subnet, in Availability Zone A
all the instances run in Availability Zone A

options.text: Replace the instances in Availability Zone A with larger instance types so that the remaining instances can carry the load when one instance fails.
options.why: Larger instances still run in one zone, so the loss of Availability Zone A still stops the whole application.

options.text: Give the Network Load Balancer a subnet in Availability Zone B as well, so that it has a load balancer node in each of the two zones.
options.why: When you enable a zone, Elastic Load Balancing [creates a load balancer node](../facts/elb.md#elb-node-per-enabled-az) there, so clients keep an entry point if Availability Zone A fails.

options.text: Turn on cross-zone load balancing for the target group so that the load balancer node in Availability Zone A can also use targets in other zones.
options.why: Cross-zone load balancing uses the [registered targets in all enabled Availability Zones](../facts/elb.md#elb-cross-zone-what-it-does), and here one zone is enabled and holds every instance.
options.misconception: believes that cross-zone load balancing reaches zones that the load balancer does not have

options.text: Run instances in Availability Zone B as well, for example with an Auto Scaling group that spans both zones and registers its instances with the target group.
options.why: AWS asks you to [avoid single points of failure, including the underlying physical infrastructure](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-wa-rel10-bp01-avoid-single-points-of-failure); instances in a second zone do that for the targets.

options.text: Create a second Network Load Balancer with a subnet in Availability Zone B, and use Amazon Route 53 failover records to switch clients between the two load balancers.
options.why: It works with instances in both zones, but it adds a second load balancer and DNS failover records, where one load balancer with two zones does the same.

items.explanation: If Availability Zone A fails, everything in it stops, so the load balancer and the targets both need a second zone. When a zone has no healthy target, the Network Load Balancer removes the address of the [corresponding subnet from DNS](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-unhealthy-az-removed-from-dns-fail-open), and clients reach the node in the healthy zone.
items.takeaway: To survive a zone failure, the load balancer needs a node and healthy targets in a second zone.
items.twin: If the stem said "the instances already run in both zones" instead: enable the second zone alone, because until then [these registered targets do not receive traffic](../facts/elb.md#elb-targets-in-disabled-az-no-traffic).
items.say: A load balancer in one zone is still one zone, so add a second zone to the load balancer and put instances there.

solvers.stem_only: Enable a second Availability Zone on the NLB (add a subnet in AZ B so it has a node there) and run instances in AZ B too, for example an Auto Scaling group across both zones registered with the target group.

items.stem: A company hosts three websites, example.com, example.net and example.org, on Amazon EC2 instances behind one Application Load Balancer. Host-based listener rules send the requests of each website to its own target group. The company must now encrypt the traffic in transit between users and the load balancer, and every website must stay on port 443. Each website has its own public certificate in AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: every website must stay on port 443

options.text: Create HTTPS listeners on ports 443, 8443 and 9443, one per website, and attach that website's ACM certificate to each.
options.why: Every website must stay on port 443, and one listener can serve them all, because a certificate list can [provide a different certificate for each domain](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sni-certificate-list-multiple-domains).

options.text: Create three Application Load Balancers, one per website, each with an HTTPS listener on port 443 and that website's ACM certificate.
options.why: Three load balancers mean three listeners and three sets of rules to run and change, where one listener with a certificate list is enough.

options.text: Replace the load balancer with a Network Load Balancer with a TCP listener on port 443, and install each website's certificate on the instances.
options.why: A Network Load Balancer works at [Layer 4](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-layer-per-type), so the host-based rules are lost, and every instance then needs its own certificates.
options.misconception: moves TLS to the instances and expects the host-based rules to keep working

options.text: Create one HTTPS listener on port 443, and add all three ACM certificates to the certificate list of that listener.
options.why: A certificate list lets one listener [support multiple domains on the same port](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sni-certificate-list-multiple-domains) and choose with a [smart certificate selection algorithm with support for SNI](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sni-certificate-list-multiple-domains).

items.explanation: The three names have different parent domains, so one wildcard certificate does not cover them. One HTTPS listener holds a default certificate plus a certificate list, and [SNI is automatically enabled](../facts/elb.md#elb-faq-sni-automatic-multiple-certificates) when the listener has [more than one TLS certificate](../facts/elb.md#elb-faq-sni-automatic-multiple-certificates). The load balancer reads the host name that the client sends and presents the matching certificate.
items.takeaway: Several HTTPS domains on one port: one listener with a certificate list, and SNI picks the certificate.
items.twin: If the stem said "shop.example.com, help.example.com and news.example.com" instead: one certificate could cover all three, because you can [use a wildcard certificate](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-cert-wildcard-or-san-single-cert).
items.say: One HTTPS listener takes a list of certificates, and SNI picks the right one for each host name.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead.

I mark the constraints: three websites with different parent domains, host rules on one load balancer, encryption in transit to the load balancer, port 443 for every website, and one ACM certificate for each website.

Before I look at the options, I predict one HTTPS listener on port 443 with all three certificates, because a certificate list lets one listener serve several domains on the same port, and SNI picks the certificate.
I remove the listeners on ports 8443 and 9443, because every website must stay on port 443. I remove the Network Load Balancer, because it works at layer 4 and would lose the host rules.

Between the certificate list and three load balancers, the difference is how much the team must run and change; the stem says LEAST operational overhead, so one listener with one set of rules wins over three load balancers with three listeners.
Check: the certificate list keeps port 443, keeps the host rules and uses the three ACM certificates. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: Add one HTTPS listener on port 443 to the existing ALB, attach all three ACM certificates to it (SNI chooses the right one by host name), and keep the host-based rules.

items.stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances that are registered in an Application Load Balancer target group with the default health check settings. The application also has a /health page that its monitoring tool calls; the page returns HTTP 200 only when the application can serve requests. After a release, the application currently answers requests for the path / with an HTTP 302 redirect to a sign-in page. Every target is now marked unhealthy, but users can still use the website. The company must ensure that the health checks show the real state of each target. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: Every target is now marked unhealthy, but users can still use the website

options.text: Make no change, because the load balancer stops sending requests to unhealthy targets, so the health checks already protect the users.
options.why: With every target unhealthy, [the load balancer fails open](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-fail-open-all-unhealthy) and [routes requests to all those targets](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-fail-open-all-unhealthy), so the checks protect nobody.

options.text: Change the health check protocol of the target group to TCP so that a target counts as healthy when it accepts a connection.
options.why: For an Application Load Balancer health check, [the possible protocols are HTTP and HTTPS](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-health-check-protocol-default-http), so a TCP check is not an option.
options.misconception: believes that an Application Load Balancer target group can use a TCP health check

options.text: Change the health check path of the target group from / to /health, and keep the default success code of the health check.
options.why: The check passes on the success code, and [the default value is 200](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-health-check-success-code-default-200); the /health page returns 200 only while the application works.

options.text: Change the application so that the path / returns HTTP 200 instead of a redirect, and release the new version to every instance.
options.why: It works, but it changes application code and needs a new release, where one target group setting fixes the check.

items.explanation: The health check requests the path /, and for the success code [the default value is 200](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-health-check-success-code-default-200). The application now answers / with 302, so every check fails. Users still get pages because, with every target unhealthy at once, [the load balancer fails open](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-fail-open-all-unhealthy). The /health page already exists, so one target group setting makes the check report the real state of each target.
items.takeaway: All targets unhealthy but the site still works: the ALB failed open, so fix the health check path or success codes.
items.twin: If the stem said "the application has no page that reports its health" instead: add 302 to the success codes, which can be [200 to 499](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-health-check-success-code-default-200).
items.say: The check expects 200 and gets a 302, so point it at the health page; the load balancer only failed open.

solvers.stem_only: The default ALB health check uses path / and success code 200, so the 302 redirect makes every target fail; with all targets unhealthy the ALB fails open and still routes to all of them. Point the target group health check at the existing /health page, which returns 200 only when the application can serve requests. No application change, and not a TCP check (that would not show application state).

items.stem: A company has several VPCs in one AWS Region and a central security VPC. Security policy requires that all traffic into and out of each VPC passes through a fleet of third-party firewall appliances that run on Amazon EC2 instances. The fleet must be scalable as traffic grows, and the company wants to centrally manage the appliances. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: all traffic into and out of each VPC

options.text: Create a Gateway Load Balancer for the appliances in the security VPC, add Gateway Load Balancer endpoints in each VPC, and route traffic to the endpoints.
options.why: With endpoints, the appliances [can reside in different AWS accounts and VPCs](../facts/elb.md#elb-gwlb-faq-endpoint-centralize-appliances), and each route table sends traffic to an endpoint [as the next hop in the route table](../facts/elb.md#elb-gwlb-endpoint-next-hop-route-table).

options.text: Create a Network Load Balancer for the appliances in the security VPC, and point every client and application at the DNS name of that load balancer.
options.why: Traffic between other hosts is not sent to the load balancer's name, so it bypasses the appliances; inline appliances need a load balancer that is [invisible to the source and destination](../facts/elb.md#elb-gwlb-faq-when-inline-appliances).

options.text: Create an Application Load Balancer with an AWS WAF web ACL in each VPC, and send all inbound web requests through that load balancer.
options.why: AWS WAF can [block, allow, or monitor (count) web requests](../facts/elb.md#elb-waf-integrates-with-alb) to the load balancer, but the policy requires third-party appliances for all traffic of each VPC.
options.misconception: treats a web application firewall for HTTP requests as inspection of all traffic

options.text: Create a separate Gateway Load Balancer and a separate fleet of appliances in each VPC, and route the traffic of each VPC through its own fleet.
options.why: It works, but a load balancer and a fleet in every VPC multiply the appliances to patch and scale, where endpoints share one central fleet.

items.explanation: The traffic is not addressed to the appliances, so this is a Gateway Load Balancer case: it is for [deploying inline virtual appliances](../facts/elb.md#elb-gwlb-faq-when-inline-appliances) and [transparently passes all Layer 3 traffic](../facts/elb.md#elb-gwlb-faq-when-inline-appliances) through them. Endpoints in each VPC receive the traffic from route tables, and the appliances stay [centralized in one location](../facts/elb.md#elb-gwlb-faq-endpoint-centralize-appliances).
items.takeaway: All traffic through third-party appliances, steered by route tables: a Gateway Load Balancer with endpoints in each VPC.
items.twin: If the stem said "filter the HTTP requests to the company's web application" instead: an Application Load Balancer with an AWS WAF web ACL, because it can [block, allow, or monitor (count) web requests](../facts/elb.md#elb-waf-integrates-with-alb).
items.say: Inline firewalls mean a Gateway Load Balancer, and route tables send each VPC's traffic to its endpoint.

solvers.stem_only: Gateway Load Balancer with the appliance fleet as targets in the central security VPC, Gateway Load Balancer endpoints (PrivateLink) in each spoke VPC, and route tables that send traffic through the endpoints.

items.stem: A company is moving an HTTP web application to Amazon EC2 instances that run across multiple Availability Zones in one AWS Region. Business partners call the application from their own networks over the internet. The company needs one entry point in front of the instances that keeps serving requests when an instance fails. Requests for /api/* must go to a separate group of instances. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
keywords: Requests for /api/* must go to a separate group of instances

options.text: Create an Application Load Balancer with a listener rule that forwards /api/* requests to a second target group and all other requests to the first target group.
options.why: Path conditions let the load balancer [forward requests based on the URL](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-path-conditions-smaller-services), so /api/* requests reach their own target group through one load balancer.

options.text: Create a Network Load Balancer with one Elastic IP address in each subnet and a TCP listener that forwards all requests to one target group of the instances.
options.why: A Network Load Balancer works at [Layer 4](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-layer-per-type) and picks a target [using a flow hash algorithm](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-flow-hash-target-selection), so it cannot send /api/* requests to a separate group.

options.text: Create a Network Load Balancer with one Elastic IP address in each subnet, and register as its target an Application Load Balancer that has a /api/* listener rule.
options.why: It works, but the company pays for two load balancers, and each one is billed for [each hour or partial hour](../facts/elb.md#elb-partial-hour-billed-as-full-hour) that it runs.

options.text: Create an Application Load Balancer, associate one Elastic IP address with its node in each subnet, and forward all requests to one target group of the instances.
options.why: The feature table lists [IP address - Static, Elastic](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-static-elastic-ip-nlb-only) for the Network Load Balancer only, so an Application Load Balancer node takes no Elastic IP address.

items.explanation: The load balancer has to read the URL of each request. An Application Load Balancer [functions at the application layer](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-layer-7), and a listener rule with a [path-pattern](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-condition-types) condition sends /api/* requests to a second target group. One load balancer does the whole job, so it is also the cheapest design.
items.takeaway: Routing by URL path needs Application Load Balancer listener rules, and one ALB can serve several target groups.
items.twin: If the stem said "the addresses must never change" instead: a Network Load Balancer with Elastic IP addresses, because you can [optionally associate one Elastic IP address](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-static-ip-per-az-optional-eip) for each zone [when you create the Network Load Balancer](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-static-ip-per-az-optional-eip).
items.say: The /api rule needs layer 7, so one Application Load Balancer with a second target group is the answer.

solvers.stem_only: One internet-facing Application Load Balancer across the AZs with a path-based listener rule sending /api/* to a second target group and the default action to the main target group.

items.stem: A company runs an API on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer in one VPC. Listener rules send /orders/* and /reports/* to separate target groups. A large customer now requires a fixed set of IP addresses that it can allow-list in its firewall. The path-based routing must stay in place, and the company uses one AWS Region. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: requires a fixed set of IP addresses
The path-based routing must stay in place

options.text: Replace the Application Load Balancer with a Network Load Balancer that has an Elastic IP address in each subnet, and move the path rules to its listener.
options.why: A Network Load Balancer works at [Layer 4](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-layer-per-type) and picks a target [using a flow hash algorithm](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-flow-hash-target-selection), so it has no /orders/* or /reports/* path rules.

options.text: Associate an Elastic IP address with the Application Load Balancer node in each subnet, and give the customer those addresses to allow-list.
options.why: The feature table lists [IP address - Static, Elastic](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-static-elastic-ip-nlb-only) for the Network Load Balancer only, so an Application Load Balancer node takes no Elastic IP address.

options.text: Create a Network Load Balancer with an Elastic IP address in each subnet, and register the existing Application Load Balancer as its target.
options.why: To give ALB routing fixed addresses, you [forward traffic from your Network Load Balancer](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-alb-target-static-ip-privatelink) to it, and the ALB [takes over the load balancing decision](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-alb-target-combines-features).

options.text: Launch Amazon EC2 instances with Elastic IP addresses that run reverse proxy software, and have them forward every request to the Application Load Balancer.
options.why: It works, but the company has to patch, scale and replace the proxy instances itself, where a managed Network Load Balancer does the same job.

items.explanation: The customer needs fixed addresses, and the API still needs rules that read the URL. A Network Load Balancer gives [static IP addresses](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-alb-target-static-ip-privatelink) and forwards to an ALB-type target group, where the ALB keeps its path rules. Both load balancers must be [in the same VPC](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-alb-target-same-vpc-same-account), which the stem gives.
items.takeaway: Fixed IP addresses plus path rules: put a Network Load Balancer with Elastic IP addresses in front of the ALB.
items.twin: If the stem said "the company uses two AWS Regions" instead: AWS Global Accelerator, because it gives [static IP addresses that serve as fixed endpoints](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-global-accelerator-static-ips) for [load balancers in one or more AWS Regions](../facts/elb.md#elb-ga-alb-multiple-regions).
items.say: Keep the Application Load Balancer for the path rules, and put a Network Load Balancer with Elastic IP addresses in front of it.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead.
I mark the constraints: the customer needs a fixed set of IP addresses, the /orders/* and /reports/* path rules must stay, and everything runs in one VPC in one Region.
Before I look at the options, I predict a swap: replace the Application Load Balancer with a Network Load Balancer, because the Network Load Balancer is the type with static and Elastic IP addresses.

I remove the Elastic IP addresses on the Application Load Balancer nodes, because the feature table gives static and Elastic IP addresses to the Network Load Balancer only. I remove the proxy instances, because the company would have to run and patch them.

Between the swap and a Network Load Balancer in front of the Application Load Balancer, the difference is the path rules. My first idea breaks because a Network Load Balancer works at layer 4 and picks a target with a flow hash, so the path rules would be lost. The stem says the rules must stay, so I keep the Application Load Balancer as the target of the Network Load Balancer.
Check: the Elastic IP addresses stay fixed, the Application Load Balancer keeps its rules, and both load balancers sit in the same VPC of one account. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: Put a Network Load Balancer with an Elastic IP per subnet in front of the existing ALB using an ALB-type target group; the ALB keeps its path rules and the customer allow-lists the NLB's static IPs (Global Accelerator would be the alternative).

items.stem: A company runs a three-tier application in one VPC. The internet-facing web tier runs on Amazon EC2 instances, and users must reach it through one endpoint. The web tier calls the application tier, which also runs on EC2 instances. Each tier must scale on its own. The application tier must be reachable privately from the web tier and must stay unreachable from the internet. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: must be reachable privately from the web tier
Each tier must scale on its own

options.text: Add a listener rule to the internet-facing load balancer that forwards /app/* requests to a target group of the application tier instances.
options.why: A path rule on the internet-facing load balancer lets any user on the internet reach the application tier with a /app/* request.
options.misconception: believes that a path rule keeps a tier hidden from the internet

options.text: Give the application tier instances public IP addresses in public subnets so that the internet-facing load balancer can reach them as targets.
options.why: Targets are reached [using private IP addresses](../facts/elb.md#elb-targets-need-no-public-ip), so public addresses only add exposure for the application tier.

options.text: Create an internet-facing Application Load Balancer in public subnets, and register the web tier instances in its target group.
options.why: Its nodes [have public IP addresses](../facts/elb.md#elb-internet-facing-nodes-public-ips) and accept users from the internet, and the web instances behind it can stay in private subnets.

options.text: Launch Amazon EC2 instances that run open source proxy software in private subnets, and have them spread the web tier's calls over the application tier.
options.why: It works, but the company has to run, patch and scale the proxy instances itself, which an internal load balancer avoids.

options.text: Create an internal Application Load Balancer in private subnets, register the application tier instances, and point the web tier's calls at it.
options.why: Internal nodes [have only private IP addresses](../facts/elb.md#elb-internal-nodes-private-ips-only), so only [clients with access to the VPC](../facts/elb.md#elb-internal-nodes-private-ips-only) reach the application tier.

items.explanation: AWS describes this pattern for multi-tier applications, with [both internal and internet-facing load balancers](../facts/elb.md#elb-multi-tier-internet-facing-plus-internal). The web instances register with the internet-facing load balancer and send their calls to the internal one, which forwards them to the application tier. Each tier scales behind its own load balancer, and the application tier has no public entry point.
items.takeaway: A private tier behind a public tier: an internet-facing load balancer for the web tier and an internal one for the application tier.
items.twin: If the stem said "partners on the internet also call the application tier" instead: the application tier needs an internet-facing load balancer too, because internal nodes [have only private IP addresses](../facts/elb.md#elb-internal-nodes-private-ips-only).
items.say: Users reach an internet-facing load balancer, and the web tier calls an internal one that only the VPC can reach.

solvers.stem_only: Internet-facing ALB in public subnets for the web tier, an internal ALB in private subnets for the application tier, each tier in its own Auto Scaling group; web tier calls the internal ALB's DNS name.

items.stem: A company runs a TCP service on Amazon EC2 instances behind a Network Load Balancer that was created with default settings. The instances run across multiple Availability Zones: 2 instances in Availability Zone A and 6 instances in Availability Zone B. Client connections are spread evenly over the two load balancer nodes. The 2 instances in Availability Zone A are overloaded, and the other instances are mostly idle. The company must spread connections evenly over all 8 instances. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: Client connections are spread evenly over the two load balancer nodes

options.text: Add 2 instances in each Availability Zone, because cross-zone load balancing is already turned on for every type of load balancer.
options.why: On a Network Load Balancer, [cross-zone load balancing is disabled by default](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-gwlb-cross-zone-off-by-default), so each node still uses the instances of its own zone, and the load stays uneven.

options.text: Turn on cross-zone load balancing for the target group, and accept the charge for data that crosses between Availability Zones.
options.why: Each node then uses the [registered targets in all enabled Availability Zones](../facts/elb.md#elb-cross-zone-what-it-does), and the data is [charged for regional data transfer between Availability Zones](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-faq-cross-zone-regional-data-transfer-charged).

options.text: Change the routing algorithm of the target group to least outstanding requests so that new connections go to the least busy instances.
options.why: A Network Load Balancer selects a target [using a flow hash algorithm](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-flow-hash-target-selection); [least outstanding requests](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-routing-algorithms-three) is an algorithm of Application Load Balancer target groups.
options.misconception: believes that a Network Load Balancer target group has the routing algorithms of an Application Load Balancer

options.text: Launch 4 more instances in Availability Zone A, and keep the same number of instances in each zone whenever the fleet changes size.
options.why: It works, but the team has to keep both zones equal at every change, where one setting spreads connections over all instances.

items.explanation: With cross-zone load balancing off, each node uses the [registered targets in its Availability Zone](../facts/elb.md#elb-cross-zone-what-it-does). The two nodes get the same number of connections, so each of the 2 instances in Availability Zone A carries three times the load of an instance in Availability Zone B. On a Network Load Balancer you can turn cross-zone load balancing [on or off at the target group level](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-cross-zone-lb-and-tg-level).
items.takeaway: Uneven instance counts per zone behind an NLB: turn on cross-zone load balancing and pay for the data between zones.
items.twin: If the stem said "an Application Load Balancer" instead: no change is needed, because cross-zone load balancing is [on by default](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-cross-zone-on-by-default) for it.
items.say: Cross-zone is off by default on a Network Load Balancer, so turn it on and accept the data transfer charge.

solvers.stem_only: NLB cross-zone load balancing is off by default; turn it on (target group or load balancer attribute) so each node spreads over all 8 targets, accepting inter-AZ data transfer charges.

items.stem: A company runs a file upload service on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. Some uploads are long-running and take up to 10 minutes. The target group uses the default deregistration delay. When the group scales in, some uploads that are still in progress on the instances that the group removes fail. The company wants minimal downtime for uploads during scale-in. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Increase the idle timeout of the load balancer to 900 seconds so that connections to the instances stay open during scale-in.
options.why: The idle timeout ends connections that stay idle; its default is [60 seconds](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-idle-timeout-default-60-seconds), and an upload that sends data is not idle.
options.misconception: confuses the idle timeout of a connection with the wait for in-flight requests during deregistration

options.text: Turn on sticky sessions for the target group so that each user's upload stays on the same instance until the upload is complete.
options.why: Sticky sessions [bind a user's session to a specific target](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sticky-sessions-what), but they do not delay the deregistration of that target during scale-in.
options.misconception: believes that stickiness keeps an instance in service until its users finish

options.text: Add a lifecycle hook to the Auto Scaling group, and run a script on each instance that completes the hook after its uploads finish.
options.why: It works, but the team has to write and maintain a script on every instance, where one target group setting waits for the uploads.

options.text: Increase the deregistration delay of the target group to 900 seconds so that in-progress uploads can finish before an instance is removed.
options.why: Deregistration lets the load balancer [help in-flight requests to the target to complete](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-deregistration-waits-for-in-flight), and the delay accepts [0 to 3600 seconds](../facts/elb.md#elb-deregistration-delay-default-300-seconds), which covers a 10-minute upload.

items.explanation: During scale-in, the load balancer [stops routing requests to a target](../facts/elb.md#elb-deregister-stops-routing-draining) that is deregistering and waits [until in-flight requests have completed](../facts/elb.md#elb-deregister-stops-routing-draining), for at most the deregistration delay. After that, [it can be terminated and replaced](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-deregistration-draining-then-unused). The delay is [300 seconds](../facts/elb.md#elb-deregistration-delay-default-300-seconds) by default, shorter than a 10-minute upload.
items.takeaway: Requests cut off during scale-in: raise the deregistration delay of the target group above the longest request.
items.twin: If the stem said "take up to 2 minutes" instead: no change is needed, because the default delay of [300 seconds](../facts/elb.md#elb-deregistration-delay-default-300-seconds) already covers the uploads.
items.say: Raise the deregistration delay above the longest upload, so draining waits for the uploads before the instance goes away.

solvers.stem_only: Raise the target group deregistration delay (connection draining) above the longest upload, for example to 900 seconds; the Auto Scaling group waits for draining before it terminates the instance.

verification.note: exam-02: swapped out for the verified level-3 item elb-q021 to bring the difficulty mix into tolerance; 2.2.K8 stays covered by elb-q011

items.stem: A company's website runs on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The HTTPS listener uses a certificate that a third-party certificate authority issued and that the company imported into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Last year the certificate expired, and the website was unavailable until an engineer imported a new certificate. The company wants to automate certificate renewal so that this outage does not happen again. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Keep the imported certificate on the listener, and rely on ACM managed renewal to renew the certificate before it expires.
options.why: ACM [does not manage the renewal process](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-imported-no-managed-renewal) for imported certificates, so the company still has to renew this one itself.

options.text: Upload the third-party certificate to IAM, and change the HTTPS listener to use the IAM certificate instead of the ACM certificate.
options.why: You can [upload the certificate](../facts/acm.md#acm-alb-certificate-from-acm-or-iam) to IAM, but that changes where it is stored, not who renews it; the company still renews it.
options.misconception: believes that a certificate in IAM renews itself

options.text: Request a public certificate for the domain from ACM, and replace the imported certificate on the HTTPS listener with it.
options.why: Certificates provided by ACM and deployed on the load balancer [can be renewed automatically](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-acm-certs-renew-automatically), and renewal [does not affect in-flight requests](../facts/acm.md#acm-alb-renewal-in-flight).

options.text: Create a scheduled AWS Lambda function that buys a new certificate from the third-party authority every year and imports it into ACM.
options.why: It works, but the company has to write and fix code that buys and imports certificates, where an ACM certificate renews itself.

items.explanation: The outage came from a manual step. For an imported certificate, ACM [does not manage the renewal process](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-imported-no-managed-renewal), and [you must monitor the expiration date](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-acm-certs-renew-automatically). A certificate that ACM issues and deploys on the load balancer [can be renewed automatically](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-acm-certs-renew-automatically), and new requests then use the renewed certificate.
items.takeaway: ACM renews the certificates it issues, not the ones you import; use an ACM certificate to automate renewal.
items.twin: If the stem said "the company must keep its current certificate authority" instead: a scheduled re-import becomes the answer, because ACM [does not manage the renewal process](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-imported-no-managed-renewal) for imported certificates.
items.say: ACM does not renew an imported certificate, so request one from ACM and let ACM renew it.

solvers.stem_only: Imported certificates are not renewed by ACM; replace it with an ACM-issued public certificate (DNS validated) so ACM renews it automatically and the listener keeps using it.

items.stem: A company is moving an HTTP web application to Amazon EC2 instances that run across multiple Availability Zones in one AWS Region. Business partners call the application from their own networks over the internet. The company needs one entry point in front of the instances that keeps serving requests when an instance fails. Each partner must allow-list the load balancer's IP addresses, and the addresses must never change. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
keywords: allow-list the load balancer's IP addresses

options.text: Create an Application Load Balancer with a listener rule that forwards /api/* requests to a second target group and all other requests to the first target group.
options.why: Elastic Load Balancing [scales your load balancer](../facts/elb.md#elb-dns-ttl-60-seconds-remap) and keeps a [time-to-live (TTL) of 60 seconds](../facts/elb.md#elb-dns-ttl-60-seconds-remap) on its DNS entry, so the [IP addresses can be remapped quickly](../facts/elb.md#elb-dns-ttl-60-seconds-remap).

options.text: Create a Network Load Balancer with one Elastic IP address in each subnet and a TCP listener that forwards all requests to one target group of the instances.
options.why: The Network Load Balancer creates a network interface in each enabled zone and [uses it to get a static IP address](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-static-ip-per-az-optional-eip); here it is an Elastic IP address.

options.text: Create a Network Load Balancer with one Elastic IP address in each subnet, and register as its target an Application Load Balancer that has a /api/* listener rule.
options.why: It gives fixed addresses too, but the extra Application Load Balancer adds a second charge for [each hour or partial hour](../facts/elb.md#elb-partial-hour-billed-as-full-hour).

options.text: Create an Application Load Balancer, associate one Elastic IP address with its node in each subnet, and forward all requests to one target group of the instances.
options.why: The feature table lists [IP address - Static, Elastic](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-static-elastic-ip-nlb-only) for the Network Load Balancer only, so an Application Load Balancer node takes no Elastic IP address.

items.explanation: The partners need fixed addresses. In the AWS feature table, [IP address - Static, Elastic](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-static-elastic-ip-nlb-only) belongs to the Network Load Balancer. In each zone, Elastic Load Balancing creates a network interface and [uses it to get a static IP address](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-static-ip-per-az-optional-eip), while an ALB's node [IP addresses can be remapped quickly](../facts/elb.md#elb-dns-ttl-60-seconds-remap). No HTTP routing is needed, so one load balancer is enough.
items.takeaway: Fixed IP addresses for a partner allow-list point to a Network Load Balancer with Elastic IP addresses.
items.twin: If the stem said "Requests for /api/* must go to a separate group of instances" instead: an Application Load Balancer with a path rule, because it can [forward requests based on the URL](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-path-conditions-smaller-services).
items.say: Partners need fixed addresses, so a Network Load Balancer with Elastic IP addresses; an ALB's addresses change.

solvers.stem_only: Network Load Balancer with an Elastic IP in each subnet (static IPs) and a TCP listener forwarding to one target group of the instances; no path routing is needed, so no ALB behind it.

items.stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in two Availability Zones. Clients connect over HTTPS on port 443 through a new load balancer. The company wants to protect the data in transit on every network hop. The load balancer must route each request to a target group by its URL path. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST secure way?
keywords: protect the data in transit on every network hop
route each request to a target group by its URL path

options.text: Use an Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener that has an ACM certificate, and forward the requests to an HTTP target group of the instances on port 80.
options.why: The HTTPS listener uses its certificate to [terminate the front-end connection](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-https-listener-terminates-and-decrypts), so the hop to the instances carries plain HTTP.

options.text: Use an Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener that has an ACM certificate, and forward the requests to an HTTPS target group of the instances, which hold certificates.
options.why: The listener decrypts to read the path, and the HTTPS target group opens a second TLS connection, so both network hops are encrypted.

options.text: Use a Network Load Balancer with a TCP listener on port 443, and forward the connections to a TCP target group of the instances, which hold certificates.
options.why: A Network Load Balancer works at [Layer 4](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-layer-per-type) and passes the encrypted bytes through, so it cannot read the URL path to choose a target group.

options.text: Use a Network Load Balancer with a TLS listener that has an ACM certificate, and forward the connections to a TLS target group of the instances, which hold certificates.
options.why: A TLS listener decrypts, but a Network Load Balancer still works at [Layer 4](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-layer-per-type) and does not read the URL path.
options.misconception: believes that a TLS listener lets a Network Load Balancer route requests by path

items.explanation: The path rule needs a [Layer 7](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-layer-per-type) load balancer, so the choice is an Application Load Balancer. Its HTTPS listener uses its certificate to [terminate the front-end connection](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-https-listener-terminates-and-decrypts) and read the request. An HTTPS target group then opens a second TLS connection to each instance, so both hops are encrypted. [The load balancer does not validate these certificates](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-target-https-no-cert-validation), so self-signed ones work.
items.takeaway: Path routing needs an Application Load Balancer; an HTTPS target group encrypts the hop to the instances.
items.twin: If the stem said "Each instance must decrypt the client traffic with its own certificate and private key" instead: the Network Load Balancer with a TCP listener on port 443, because it [passes encrypted traffic through to the targets](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-https-decrypt-at-target-use-nlb-tcp).
items.say: Path rules need an ALB; give it an HTTPS target group, so the hop to the instances is encrypted too.

solvers.stem_only: ALB (needed for path routing) with an HTTPS listener using an ACM certificate, forwarding to HTTPS target groups so traffic is re-encrypted from the ALB to the instances.

items.stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. The application keeps each user's session data in the memory of the instance that served the user's first request. Users are signed out when a later request reaches a different instance. The company wants a fix as soon as possible, with minimal code changes. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: session data in the memory of the instance
as soon as possible, with minimal code changes

options.text: Turn on duration-based stickiness for the target group, so that the load balancer sends all requests of a user to the same instance.
options.why: Sticky sessions [bind a user's session to a specific target](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sticky-sessions-what) through a load balancer cookie, with no code change.

options.text: Store the session data in an Amazon ElastiCache cluster that every instance reads and writes, and change the application to use the cluster.
options.why: It works and is the better long-term design, but it needs code changes and a new cluster, so it is not the fastest fix.

options.text: Replace the Application Load Balancer with a Network Load Balancer, and turn on source IP stickiness for the target group of the instances.
options.why: It replaces the load balancer, and source IP stickiness can cause [uneven distribution of connections and flows](../facts/elb.md#elb-sticky-uneven-load-nat) when many users share one NAT address.
options.misconception: believes that source IP stickiness of a Network Load Balancer is the same as cookie stickiness

options.text: Run a session database on one new EC2 instance that every web instance reads and writes, and change the application to use that database.
options.why: It needs code changes, and the team patches and scales the database instance itself, which is more work than one target group setting.

items.explanation: Sticky sessions [bind a user's session to a specific target](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sticky-sessions-what), so each user returns to the instance that holds the session in memory. The target group offers [duration-based cookies and application-based cookies](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sticky-duration-vs-application-cookie); both kinds send a user back to one target, and the duration-based kind needs no cookie from the application. It is one setting on the target group, so the fix is live quickly and needs no code.
items.takeaway: For a fast fix without code changes, turn on stickiness for the target group.
items.twin: If the stem said "Users must keep their sessions when an instance is terminated, so the web tier must become stateless and scalable" instead: ElastiCache, because AWS calls a [centralized session management data store](../facts/elb.md#elb-session-store-centralized-not-on-servers) the ideal answer.
items.say: Turn on duration-based stickiness on the target group; users return to their instance, and nobody changes code.

solvers.stem_only: Quick fix without code change: enable sticky sessions (duration-based load balancer cookie) on the ALB target group.

items.stem: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances in public subnets. The instances have public IP addresses and are registered as instance targets of an internet-facing Network Load Balancer with a TCP listener on port 443. The load balancer was created years ago without security groups. The instances' security group allows TCP port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. The company must restrict access so that the instances accept traffic on port 443 from a load balancer and from no other source. Clients must keep reaching the application through a load balancer. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST secure way?
keywords: created years ago without security groups
from a load balancer and from no other source

options.text: Associate a new security group with the existing Network Load Balancer, and allow port 443 on the instances only from that security group.
options.why: The load balancer was created without security groups, and for such a load balancer [you can't associate them](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-security-groups-only-at-creation) later.
options.misconception: believes that security groups can be added to any Network Load Balancer later

options.text: Keep the rule that allows port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0, because a Network Load Balancer has no security group that a target rule can reference.
options.why: A Network Load Balancer can get security groups [when you create it](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-security-groups-only-at-creation), so targets can reference one; this option restricts nothing.

options.text: Move the instances to private subnets without public IP addresses, and keep the rule that allows port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 on the instances.
options.why: Private subnets remove the internet path, but any resource in the VPC can still reach port 443 on the instances, so they accept traffic from more than a load balancer.

options.text: Create a new Network Load Balancer with a security group, allow port 443 on the instances only from that security group, and move clients to it.
options.why: Targets that allow the load balancer's security group accept clients [through your Network Load Balancer](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-sg-reference-blocks-direct-access) and refuse direct traffic.

items.explanation: A Network Load Balancer gets security groups [when you create it](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-security-groups-only-at-creation); for one created without them, [you can't associate them](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-security-groups-only-at-creation) later. A new load balancer with a security group lets the instance rule name [the load balancer's security group as the source](../facts/elb.md#elb-target-sg-reference-lb-sg). Clients then reach the instances [through your Network Load Balancer](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-sg-reference-blocks-direct-access), and the rule [prevents them from sending traffic directly](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-sg-reference-blocks-direct-access).
items.takeaway: A Network Load Balancer gets security groups at creation; to add them later, create a new load balancer.
items.twin: If the stem said "the load balancer was created with a security group" instead: keep it and reference its security group in the instance rule, because you can [change the security groups](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-security-groups-only-at-creation) of such a load balancer.
items.say: That old NLB can't get a security group now, so create a new one with a security group and let the instances trust only that group.

solvers.stem_only: Security groups can be associated with a Network Load Balancer only when it is created; an NLB created without security groups cannot get one later. So create a new NLB with a security group, allow port 443 on the instances only from that security group, and move clients to the new load balancer. Private subnets alone with 0.0.0.0/0 would still allow any source that can route to the instances.

items.stem: A company serves a website through an Application Load Balancer that has an HTTPS listener on port 443 with an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate. The load balancer has no other listener. Users who enter the website address with HTTP in the browser receive an error. The company wants these users to reach the HTTPS site, so that all requests are encrypted in transit. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: The load balancer has no other listener

options.text: Add an HTTP listener on port 80 that forwards requests to the instances, and change the application code to return a redirect to HTTPS.
options.why: It works, but the team writes, tests and deploys code for a redirect that the load balancer can return by itself.

options.text: Add an HTTP listener on port 80 whose default action returns a fixed response that asks users to enter the HTTPS address in the browser.
options.why: A fixed-response action [returns a custom HTTP response](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-fixed-response-action) and drops the request, so users still have to retype the address.
options.misconception: believes that a fixed response can move the user to HTTPS

options.text: Add an HTTP listener on port 80 whose default action redirects every request to HTTPS on port 443 with a permanent HTTP 301 response.
options.why: A redirect action can send [HTTP to HTTPS](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-redirect-http-to-https) as a [permanent (HTTP 301)](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-redirect-http-to-https) redirect, so the browser repeats the request over TLS.

options.text: Create a second Application Load Balancer with an HTTP listener on port 80, and point a second DNS name for the website at that load balancer.
options.why: One load balancer can listen on [HTTP port 80](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-faq-http-and-https-one-alb) and [HTTPS port 443](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-faq-http-and-https-one-alb), and users would not type a second name anyway.
options.misconception: believes that one load balancer cannot serve both HTTP and HTTPS

items.explanation: One Application Load Balancer can have listeners on [HTTP port 80](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-faq-http-and-https-one-alb) and [HTTPS port 443](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-faq-http-and-https-one-alb). A redirect action on the new port 80 listener sends [HTTP to HTTPS](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-redirect-http-to-https), so the browser repeats the request over TLS. The load balancer does the work, and the application code stays unchanged.
items.takeaway: An HTTP listener with a redirect action moves users to HTTPS without code changes.
items.twin: If the stem said "users of the HTTPS site must be sent to an old HTTP site" instead: no redirect action fits, because [You cannot redirect HTTPS to HTTP](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-redirect-http-to-https).
items.say: Add a port 80 listener whose default action redirects to HTTPS; the load balancer does it, not the code.

solvers.stem_only: Add an HTTP listener on port 80 with a redirect action to HTTPS port 443 (HTTP 301).

items.stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in three Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer. Cross-zone load balancing is turned off for the target group, and zonal shift is turned on for the load balancer. During an incident, responses from the instances in one Availability Zone become slow, but those instances still pass their health checks. The company must move traffic away from that Availability Zone as soon as possible. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: move traffic away from that Availability Zone

options.text: Start a zonal shift in Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) for the load balancer, away from the Availability Zone with the slow instances.
options.why: Zonal shift moves the load balancer's traffic [away from an impaired Availability Zone](../facts/elb.md#elb-zonal-shift-what) to the healthy zones, and it takes one action.

options.text: Wait for the target group health checks to mark the slow instances as unhealthy, so that the load balancer stops routing requests to them.
options.why: The instances pass their checks, and the load balancer [routes traffic only to the healthy targets](../facts/elb.md#elb-routes-only-to-healthy-targets), so it keeps sending them requests.
options.misconception: believes that slow targets fail their health checks

options.text: Deregister the instances in that Availability Zone from the target group one at a time, and register them again after the incident ends.
options.why: It works, but every target is a manual step, and by default the load balancer [waits 300 seconds](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-deregistration-waits-for-in-flight) before it completes each deregistration.

options.text: Create a new Application Load Balancer in the two healthy Availability Zones, register their instances, and point the DNS record of the website at it.
options.why: It works in the end, but a new load balancer, its listeners and a DNS change take longer than one action on the current load balancer.

items.explanation: Zonal shift, a capability of [Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC)](../facts/elb.md#elb-zonal-shift-what), moves traffic [away from an impaired Availability Zone](../facts/elb.md#elb-zonal-shift-what) [with a single action](../facts/elb.md#elb-zonal-shift-what). For a load balancer with cross-zone load balancing turned off, AWS Well-Architected names ARC [to provide zonal shift capability](../facts/elb.md#elb-wa-rel10-cross-zone-off-use-zonal-shift). The two other zones keep serving. Health checks do not help, because the slow instances still pass them.
items.takeaway: To drain one impaired Availability Zone fast, start a zonal shift on the load balancer.
items.twin: If the stem said "AWS should move the traffic when its own monitoring finds an impaired zone" instead: zonal autoshift, because then [you authorize AWS to shift away resource traffic](../facts/elb.md#elb-zonal-autoshift-aws-shifts).
items.say: Start a zonal shift on the load balancer; one action moves traffic out of the bad zone, even though health checks still pass.

solvers.stem_only: Start an ARC zonal shift for the ALB away from the impaired Availability Zone.

items.stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in two Availability Zones. Clients connect over HTTPS on port 443 through a new load balancer. The company wants to protect the data in transit on every network hop. The TLS session that each client opens must end on an instance, which decrypts the traffic with its own certificate and private key. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST secure way?
keywords: protect the data in transit on every network hop

options.text: Use an Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener that has an ACM certificate, and forward the requests to an HTTP target group of the instances on port 80.
options.why: The HTTPS listener uses its certificate to [terminate the front-end connection](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-https-listener-terminates-and-decrypts), so the instances receive plain HTTP and decrypt nothing.

options.text: Use an Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener that has an ACM certificate, and forward the requests to an HTTPS target group of the instances, which hold certificates.
options.why: The listener has to [terminate the front-end connection](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-https-listener-terminates-and-decrypts) first, so the client's TLS session ends at the load balancer, and the data is plain text inside it.
options.misconception: believes that re-encryption keeps the data hidden from the load balancer

options.text: Use a Network Load Balancer with a TCP listener on port 443, and forward the connections to a TCP target group of the instances, which hold certificates.
options.why: A TCP listener on port 443 [passes encrypted traffic through to the targets](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-https-decrypt-at-target-use-nlb-tcp), so each instance ends the client's TLS session with its own certificate.

options.text: Use a Network Load Balancer with a TLS listener that has an ACM certificate, and forward the connections to a TLS target group of the instances, which hold certificates.
options.why: A TLS listener ends the client's session at the load balancer; for decryption on the targets, AWS says to [create a TCP listener on port 443](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-tls-listener-terminate-tcp-passthrough).
options.misconception: believes that a TLS listener passes the encrypted traffic through

items.explanation: The client's TLS session has to end on the instance. When the targets have to decrypt, AWS points to [a Network Load Balancer with a TCP listener on port 443](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-https-decrypt-at-target-use-nlb-tcp), which [passes encrypted traffic through to the targets](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-https-decrypt-at-target-use-nlb-tcp). Both Application Load Balancer options and the TLS listener end the client's session at the load balancer.
items.takeaway: For TLS that ends on the instances, use a TCP listener on port 443 of a Network Load Balancer.
items.twin: If the stem said "The load balancer must route each request by its URL path, and every hop must stay encrypted" instead: the Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS target group, because a Network Load Balancer works at [Layer 4](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-layer-per-type).
items.say: If the instances must decrypt, use a Network Load Balancer with a TCP listener on 443; it passes TLS through untouched.

solvers.stem_only: The client's TLS session must end on the instance, so the load balancer must not terminate TLS: use a Network Load Balancer with a TCP listener on port 443 (TLS passthrough) to a TCP target group, and let each instance decrypt with its own certificate and private key. An ALB HTTPS listener or an NLB TLS listener terminates the client session at the load balancer, even if it re-encrypts to the targets.

items.stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. The application keeps each user's session data in the memory of the instance that served the user's first request. Users are signed out when a later request reaches a different instance. Users must keep their sessions when an instance is terminated, so the web tier must become stateless and scalable. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: session data in the memory of the instance
keep their sessions when an instance is terminated

options.text: Turn on duration-based stickiness for the target group, so that the load balancer sends all requests of a user to the same instance.
options.why: Sticky sessions [bind a user's session to a specific target](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sticky-sessions-what), so the session is lost with that instance at scale-in.

options.text: Store the session data in an Amazon ElastiCache cluster that every instance reads and writes, and change the application to use the cluster.
options.why: A [centralized session management data store](../facts/elb.md#elb-session-store-centralized-not-on-servers) keeps sessions outside the instances, so any instance can serve any user after scale-in.

options.text: Replace the Application Load Balancer with a Network Load Balancer, and turn on source IP stickiness for the target group of the instances.
options.why: Source IP stickiness still keeps the session on one instance, and it can cause [uneven distribution of connections and flows](../facts/elb.md#elb-sticky-uneven-load-nat).
options.misconception: believes that source IP stickiness keeps sessions when an instance goes away

options.text: Run a session database on one new EC2 instance that every web instance reads and writes, and change the application to use that database.
options.why: It works, but the team patches and scales one self-managed database instance, and that instance becomes a single point of failure for every session.

items.explanation: To make a web tier stateless, AWS says to offload session data to a [database, cache, or external files](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-wa-offload-session-data). AWS calls a [centralized session management data store](../facts/elb.md#elb-session-store-centralized-not-on-servers) the ideal solution [when your fleet of web servers is elastic](../facts/elb.md#elb-session-store-centralized-not-on-servers). A managed ElastiCache cluster keeps the sessions when Auto Scaling terminates an instance, and the team runs no database instance of its own.
items.takeaway: To keep sessions through scale-in, move them to a shared store such as ElastiCache; stickiness does not keep them.
items.twin: If the stem said "The company wants a fix as soon as possible, with minimal code changes" instead: duration-based stickiness, because sticky sessions [bind a user's session to a specific target](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sticky-sessions-what) without code changes.
items.say: Move the sessions to ElastiCache; then any instance can serve any user, and scale-in loses nothing.

solvers.stem_only: Externalize session state to a shared managed store, for example Amazon ElastiCache (or DynamoDB), and change the app to read and write sessions there; no stickiness needed.
